fieldMarks: Long, slender snake (to about 1.8 m); adults over about 800 mm are uniform gray-green, green or yellowish-green above.
Belly white to yellowish and unmarked; head elongated and broader than the neck, tail long (23-37% of total length), anal plate divided.
Hatchlings and juveniles are tan or gray with dark blotches that fade with age.
behavior: Active mostly mid-March to late November in Arizona; diurnal and crepuscular.
Both terrestrial and arboreal; uses rock crevices or burrows for shelter.
Eats mainly rodents, also other small mammals, birds and lizards, killed by constriction.
habitat: Montane woodland and chaparral, in Arizona mostly oak woodland and savanna and adjoining semidesert grassland, often on rocky canyons with water.
range: Northern edge of a largely tropical range: southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico in the United States (state rank S1, state-threatened in New Mexico), south to Costa Rica; not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Glossy snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Juvenile green ratsnakes resemble glossy snakes, but glossy snakes lack the elongated head and have an undivided anal plate (Tucson Herpetological Society).

lookalikes.name: Coachwhip
lookalikes.howToTell: Young coachwhips have 17 scale rows at midbody and no elongated head distinct from the neck (Tucson Herpetological Society).
